title: The Discovery of Penicillin
summary: How a Scottish scientist named Alexander Fleming accidentally discovered penicillin, the world's first widely used antibiotic, when mold grew on a forgotten lab dish in 1928.
poll: Fleming's accidental discovery of penicillin is one of the luckiest accidents in the history of medicine.

versions.title: The Mold That Saves Lives
versions.text:
Have you heard of penicillin? It is a kind of medicine. It helps sick people get well.

Long ago, a small cut could turn bad. Germs could get in. People could get very sick. Some even died.

A man lived in England. His name was Fleming. He grew germs in jars. He did this for his job.

One day in 1928, he came back from a trip. He saw mold on a dish. It was green. It was fuzzy.

Fleming looked at it. The germs near the mold were dead! The mold had killed them.

He looked at the mold. It made a juice. The juice killed germs. He named it penicillin.

This was a big new medicine. Soon, doctors used it. It saved many lives.

Today, doctors still use medicines like it. They stop small cuts from turning bad.

versions.title: Fleming's Lucky Mold
versions.text:
Penicillin is a kind of medicine called an antibiotic. It helps the body fight off infections caused by bacteria, tiny germs too small to see.

Before antibiotics existed, even a small cut could turn dangerous. Bacteria could infect the wound. People could grow seriously ill. Many died from what started as a simple scrape.

A Scottish man named Alexander Fleming worked in a lab in London. He studied bacteria. He often grew them on small round dishes called petri dishes.

One day in 1928, Fleming returned from a short vacation. He noticed something strange on one of his dishes. It was a patch of green, fuzzy mold.

Fleming looked closely and made an unexpected discovery. The bacteria near the mold had died. It was as though something in the mold had destroyed them.

He studied the mold and found that it made a substance. The substance could kill bacteria. He named it penicillin, after the mold that made it.

This became the first widely used antibiotic medicine in history. Years later, other scientists found ways to make it in huge amounts. It went on to save countless lives in the Second World War.

In 1945, Fleming shared the Nobel Prize in Medicine with two scientists who helped turn his find into a usable medicine. Their names were Howard Florey and Ernst Chain.

Today, doctors around the world still use antibiotics every single day. Many of them can trace their roots back to that one lucky, forgotten dish in Fleming's small London lab.

versions.title: The Discovery of Penicillin
versions.text:
Penicillin is a type of medicine known as an antibiotic. It helps the human body fight off infections caused by bacteria, microscopic pathogens far too small to see without laboratory equipment.

Before antibiotics existed, even a minor cut could become life-threatening. Bacteria could infect the wound, and the patient could grow seriously ill. Countless people died from what had started as a simple scrape.

A Scottish bacteriologist named Alexander Fleming worked in a laboratory in London. He studied bacteria extensively, routinely growing colonies on small round dishes known as petri dishes.

One day in 1928, Fleming returned from a short vacation to his laboratory. He noticed something genuinely strange on one of his forgotten petri dishes. It was a patch of fuzzy mold known scientifically as Penicillium notatum.

Fleming examined the dish closely and made an unexpected discovery. The bacteria surrounding the mold had died completely, as though some substance within the mold had destroyed them.

He investigated further and discovered that the mold produced a chemical substance capable of killing bacteria. He named this substance penicillin, after the mold species that had produced it.

At first, Fleming struggled to produce enough penicillin to test it properly, and for years the discovery sat largely unused. This became the first widely used antibiotic in medical history only after other scientists took up the challenge. Over a decade later, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain found reliable methods for mass-producing it, saving countless lives during the Second World War.

In 1945, Fleming shared the Nobel Prize in Medicine with Florey and Chain. Together they had turned an accidental laboratory observation into a lifesaving medicine used around the world.

Today, antibiotics remain some of the most widely prescribed medicines on earth, treating infections that would once have routinely killed otherwise healthy people. Every one of them descends, in some sense, from that single forgotten dish in Fleming's London laboratory.

versions.title: The Discovery of Penicillin
versions.text:
Penicillin is a type of medicine known as an antibiotic. It helps the human body combat infections caused by bacteria, microscopic pathogens far too small to see without the equipment Fleming relied upon throughout his long and distinguished research career in London.

Before antibiotics existed, even a minor cut could become life-threatening, since bacteria could infect the wound and the patient could grow seriously, sometimes fatally, ill as a direct consequence of an infection left untreated for long enough. Hospital wards of that era regularly saw patients lost to infections that are treated routinely and easily today.

A Scottish bacteriologist named Alexander Fleming worked in a laboratory in London. He studied bacteria extensively for years, routinely cultivating colonies on small round dishes known as petri dishes for his methodical research into infection and immunity. Fleming was famously untidy, often leaving old dishes stacked across his laboratory bench for weeks before finally clearing them away.

One day in 1928, Fleming returned from a short vacation to his laboratory, and he noticed something genuinely strange on one of his forgotten petri dishes: a patch of fuzzy mold known scientifically as Penicillium notatum, growing where it had no business growing at all.

Fleming examined the dish closely and made an unexpected discovery, since the bacteria surrounding the mold had died completely, as though some substance within the mold had destroyed them on contact with the entire colony of microorganisms.

He investigated further and discovered that the mold produced a chemical substance capable of killing bacteria, a finding that struck him as scientifically remarkable, though its full, world-changing importance was not immediately apparent even to him or to most of his scientific colleagues at the time, who largely overlooked the observation at first.

At first, Fleming struggled to produce enough penicillin to test it properly, and for years the discovery sat largely unused by the wider medical community; it became the first widely used antibiotic in medical history only once other scientists took up the challenge. Over a decade later, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain found reliable methods for mass-producing it industrially at scale, saving countless lives during the Second World War and in the decades that followed.

In 1945, Fleming shared the Nobel Prize in Medicine with Florey and Chain, having together turned an accidental laboratory observation into a lifesaving medicine used throughout virtually the entire world, from rural clinics to major hospitals.

Today, antibiotics remain some of the most widely prescribed medicines on earth, treating infections that would once have routinely killed otherwise healthy people, and every one of them descends, in some real sense, from that single forgotten petri dish in Fleming's quiet London laboratory.

HIGH.modelAnswer: Before antibiotics existed, even a minor cut could become life-threatening once bacteria infected the wound, and countless people died from otherwise simple injuries. While growing bacteria colonies on petri dishes in his famously untidy London laboratory, the bacteriologist Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a forgotten dish had grown mold, and the bacteria surrounding it had died. He discovered that the mold produced a substance capable of killing bacteria, which he named penicillin, though he initially struggled to produce enough of it to realize its full potential. Over a decade later, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain developed reliable methods for mass-producing penicillin, turning Fleming's accidental observation into the first widely used antibiotic and saving countless lives during the Second World War. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine, and antibiotics descended from that discovery remain among the most widely used medicines on earth today.
